tumultuous

/too-MUL-choo-us/ — stress on second syllable, rhymes with dull · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Tumultuous describes something marked by great disorder, confusion, or emotional turmoil.

The tumultuous crowd surged and roared as the gates finally opened.

Worked Example

When the stadium gates opened for the much-anticipated concert, thousands of fans erupted in chaos — pushing, shouting, arms raised — a mass of human commotion and emotional intensity.

Tumultuous is more precise than 'loud' or 'crowded' because it captures both the physical disorder and the heightened emotional turmoil all at once. The word encompasses chaos, passion, and upheaval together.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

chaotic: Chaotic names the disorder alone - a chaotic desk, a chaotic schedule - with no particular feeling attached. Tumultuous joins that disorder to strong emotion sweeping through people: a tumultuous scene is not just a mess, it is a mess charged with passion and upheaval.

riotous: Riotous means wildly noisy, unruly, and out of control - a riotous party rattles the windows. It is all about the wildness and noise, and says nothing about the mix of feelings underneath. Tumultuous covers the same uproar and adds the emotional turmoil driving it.

frenzied: Frenzied describes fast, frantic, almost desperate activity - a frenzied search for lost keys, even by one person. Tumultuous is bigger: it needs a whole scene in upheaval, where disorder and surging emotion fill a crowd, not just one person's racing energy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

serene: completely calm, peaceful, and untroubled

orderly: arranged calmly, without noise or confusion

Where it sits · how close to total chaos — restless → agitated → turbulent → tumultuous

restless vs. tumultuous: Restless is far milder than tumultuous: a restless crowd shifts and murmurs, while a tumultuous one erupts into roaring disorder.

agitated vs. tumultuous: Agitated is stronger than restless but weaker than tumultuous; an agitated audience is visibly stirred up, yet a tumultuous one has tipped over into open chaos.

turbulent vs. tumultuous: Turbulent comes closest to tumultuous — both describe violent disturbance — but tumultuous adds the deafening noise and confusion of a scene completely out of control.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tumultu-

Root — tumultu-: uproar; noisy, violent commotion (from Latin tumultus, from tumere, 'to swell')

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: The root tumultu- means 'uproar or noisy commotion' (from Latin tumultus, from tumere, 'to swell'), and -ous means 'full of' — so tumultuous literally means 'full of uproar': a scene swollen with noise, disorder, and confusion.

Use the root in a new word: tumult

Use the root in a new word: tumult: When the referee reversed the call, a tumult of boos and shouting swallowed the stadium — the very uproar packed inside tumultuous.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / literary

Tumultuous describes scenes marked by great disorder and emotional intensity. Use it in literature and historical writing to convey not just chaos, but also the turbulent feelings and drama involved. For simple disorder or confusion, 'chaotic' is usually plainer and sufficient.
